domains.diagram:
flowchart TB
  P([Pod not working]) --> S{kubectl get pod: status?}

notes.title: Pending or Waiting pods: read Events
notes.gist: A Pending pod never got a node; a Waiting pod got one but cannot start, usually because the image will not pull.
points: Pending means no node fits: CPU or memory, taints, nodeSelector, or an unbound PVC.

`kubectl describe pod

`: the scheduler explains itself in Events at the bottom.
Waiting with ImagePullBackOff: check image name, tag, registry access and pull secret.
Stuck Terminating usually means a finalizer that a webhook stops the control plane removing.
notes.tip: Tasks say 'make the pod run'. Read Events before editing. Trap: raising resources when the real cause is a taint, a selector typo or a Pending PVC.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A([Pod not Running]) --> B{Has a node?}
  B -->|no| C[Pending: describe, read Events]
  C --> D[Resources, taints, selector, PVC]
  B -->|yes| E[Waiting: image pull failing?]
  E --> F[Fix image name, tag, secret]

notes.title: CrashLoopBackOff: read the dead container
notes.gist: The container starts, dies and is restarted with growing delays; the reason sits in the previous container's logs and exit state.
points:
`kubectl logs

--previous` shows output of the crashed instance, not the fresh one.
Restart delay grows exponentially, capped at 5 minutes by default, and resets after a stable run.
Causes: app error, wrong command or args, missing config, failing liveness or startup probe.
`kubectl describe pod`: Last State shows the exit code and reason, such as OOMKilled.
`restartPolicy` defaults to Always; Deployments allow only Always.
notes.tip: Expect 'the pod keeps restarting, find why and fix it'. Trap: reading current logs instead of `--previous`, or forgetting `-c` in multi-container pods.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Container starts] --> B[Exits or probe fails]
  B --> C[kubelet restarts it]
  C --> D[Backoff grows, max 5 min]
  D -.-> A
  B --> E[Read previous logs, Last State]

notes.objective: Manage and evaluate container output streams
notes.title: Container logs: streams, files, rotation
notes.gist: Apps write to stdout and stderr; the runtime stores that in files on the node, and kubectl logs reads them back.
points:
`kubectl logs

-c -f` follows one container; `--previous` reads the crashed one.
Node files live under `/var/log/pods`; kubelet and runtime log to journald: `journalctl -u kubelet`.
kubelet rotates at `containerLogMaxSize` 10Mi and keeps `containerLogMaxFiles` 5 by default.
`kubectl logs` returns only the newest file, so older rotated output is not shown.
A streaming sidecar can tail a log file to its own stdout for `kubectl logs`.
notes.tip: Tasks ask you to save a pod's error lines: `kubectl logs p | grep -i error > /opt/out.txt`. Trap: wrong container or namespace, or the wrong output path.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[App stdout and stderr] --> B[Container runtime]
  B --> C[(Log files in /var/log/pods)]
  C --> D[kubelet]
  D --> E[kubectl logs]
  F[Sidecar tails app log file] -.-> B

notes.title: Debug inside pods: exec and debug
notes.gist: When logs are not enough, open a shell in the container, or attach a temporary debug container if it has none.
points:
`kubectl exec -it

-- sh` runs a shell in a running container.

No shell? `kubectl debug -it

--image=busybox:1.28 --target=` adds an ephemeral container.
`--copy-to=<new>` debugs a copy; add `--set-image` or a new command, original untouched.
`kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=ubuntu` gives a node shell; host files at `/host`.
notes.tip: Use when a task says 'find the process or file' in a shell-less pod. Trap: forgetting `--` before the command, or inspecting the copy, not the original.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Image has a shell?} -->|yes| B[kubectl exec -it pod sh]
  A -->|no| C[kubectl debug: ephemeral container]
  C --> D[target: sees app processes]
  A -->|need changes| E[debug copy-to: new pod]
  F[Node problem] --> G[debug node: host at /host]

notes.objective: Troubleshoot clusters and nodes
notes.title: Node NotReady: bring the kubelet back
notes.gist: A node turns NotReady when its kubelet stops reporting: the service is stopped, misconfigured, or cannot reach the API server.
points: `kubectl describe node <n>`: conditions show Unknown, 'Kubelet stopped posting node status'.
Unreachable nodes get `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` taints with NoSchedule and NoExecute.
On the node: `systemctl status kubelet`, then `journalctl -u kubelet` for the real error.
Usual fixes: start and enable kubelet, correct a bad flag or config path, turn swap off.
After editing kubelet config: `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet`.
notes.tip: Task: 'node01 is NotReady, fix it permanently'. Trap: `systemctl start` without `enable`, so it breaks again after reboot, or fixing the wrong node over ssh.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A([Node NotReady]) --> B[describe node: conditions]
  B --> C[ssh to the node]
  C --> D{kubelet active?}
  D -->|no| E[Start and enable kubelet]
  D -->|yes, failing| F[journalctl -u kubelet: read error]
  F --> G[Fix config, daemon-reload, restart]

video.title: Troubleshooting: Node Not Ready Status

notes.objective: Troubleshoot cluster components
notes.title: Control plane down: static pod manifests
notes.gist: On kubeadm clusters the API server, etcd, scheduler and controller-manager are static pods the kubelet runs from YAML files on disk.
points: Manifests live in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`; kubelet recreates the pod when a file changes.
API server down, kubectl fails: on the node run `crictl ps -a`, `crictl logs <id>`.
Container log files under `/var/log/pods` stay readable even when the API is down.
Typical breakage: a typo in a flag, wrong cert path, wrong etcd endpoint or port.
Scheduler down: new pods stay Pending. Controller-manager down: lost pods are not replaced.
notes.tip: Task: 'the cluster stopped answering after a change, fix it'. Trap: trying `kubectl edit` on a static pod; edit the manifest file, then wait for kubelet.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[kubelet] -->|watches| B[Static pod YAML files]
  B --> C[kube-apiserver]
  B --> D[etcd]
  B --> E[kube-scheduler]
  B --> F[controller-manager]
  C -.->|down?| G[crictl ps -a, crictl logs]

notes.objective: Monitor cluster and application resource usage
notes.title: Resource usage with kubectl top
notes.gist: metrics-server collects CPU and memory from every kubelet and serves it through the Metrics API that kubectl top and the HPA read.
points: `kubectl top nodes` and `kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu` show live usage.

`kubectl top pod

--containers` splits usage per container.
No metrics-server means `kubectl top` errors: the `metrics.k8s.io` API is missing.
It shows current usage only, not history or alerts.
Compare with requests and limits under Allocated resources in `kubectl describe node`.
notes.tip: Task: 'write the pod using most CPU in namespace X to a file'. Trap: missing `-n`, or sorting by memory when the task asked for CPU.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[kubelet on each node] --> B[metrics-server]
  B --> C[Metrics API: metrics.k8s.io]
  C --> D[kubectl top]
  C --> E[HPA and VPA]

notes.objective: Troubleshoot services and networking
notes.title: Service unreachable: test hop by hop
notes.gist: Check each hop in order: the Service exists, DNS resolves it, endpoints exist, pods answer directly, then kube-proxy and policies.
points: Endpoints: `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>`; empty means a selector mismatch.
Service `targetPort` must equal the pod's `containerPort`; a mismatch is accepted without error.
Name fails but IP works: DNS problem. Test `nslookup kubernetes.default` from a pod.
Pods answer by IP but the Service does not: suspect kube-proxy and read its logs.
Failing readiness probes remove pod IPs from the endpoints.
notes.tip: Adds to the playbook's Service steps. Trap: fixing the Service when a NetworkPolicy blocks traffic, or testing a short name from another namespace.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Service exists?] --> B[DNS name resolves?]
  B --> C[EndpointSlices not empty?]
  C --> D[Pods answer on targetPort?]
  D --> E[kube-proxy and NetworkPolicy]

summary.tests: Whether you can find and fix a broken pod, node, control plane component or Service fast, using describe, logs, events and node tools.
must_know: Read Events at the bottom of `kubectl describe` before changing anything.
`kubectl logs --previous` shows why a crashed container died.
Node NotReady: `systemctl status kubelet` and `journalctl -u kubelet` on that node.
Control plane pods are static: edit files in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`, not live objects.
`kubectl top` needs metrics-server and shows current CPU and memory only.
A Service with no endpoints means its selector does not match pod labels.
Container logs rotate at 10Mi by default; only the newest file is returned.
traps: Starting the kubelet without enabling it, so it is down again after a reboot.
Reading current logs of a crash-looping container instead of `--previous`.
Working in the default namespace when the broken pod lives elsewhere.

notes.objective: Manage role based access control (RBAC)
notes.title: RBAC: roles, bindings, verify with can-i
notes.gist: A Role lists allowed verbs on resources; a binding hands that list to a user, group or ServiceAccount.
points: Role and RoleBinding are namespaced; ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding are cluster-wide.
A RoleBinding may reference a ClusterRole to grant it inside one namespace only.
`roleRef` is immutable: delete and recreate the binding to change the role.
ServiceAccount user name format: `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>`.
Check with `kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<user> -n <ns>`.
notes.tip: Typical task: a ServiceAccount may only list deployments in one namespace. Trap: a ClusterRoleBinding grants every namespace; a binding in the wrong namespace makes can-i say no.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  B[RoleBinding: one namespace] --> A[Subject: user, group, SA]
  C[ClusterRoleBinding: all namespaces] --> A
  B --> D[Role]
  B -.->|may reference| E[ClusterRole]
  C --> E

video.title: Understand Role Based Access Control in Kubernetes

notes.objective: Prepare underlying infrastructure for installing a Kubernetes cluster; Understand extension interfaces (CNI, CSI, CRI, etc.)
notes.title: Prepare nodes: runtime, CNI, kernel settings
notes.gist: Every node needs a CRI runtime, IP forwarding on and swap handled; the cluster then needs a CNI plugin for pod networking.
points: Minimum: 2 GB RAM per machine, 2 CPUs for control plane, unique hostname, MAC, product_uuid.
kubelet fails to start if swap is on: `swapoff -a` and remove swap from `/etc/fstab`.
Set `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1` in sysctl config; check with `sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward`.
Use the `systemd` cgroup driver in both kubelet and containerd (`SystemdCgroup = true`).
CRI plugs in the runtime, CNI the pod network, CSI the storage drivers.
notes.tip: Tasks may say 'prepare this node and install kubeadm'. Trap: kubelet and runtime cgroup drivers differ, or forgetting `apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  N[Linux node] --> S[Swap off, IP forwarding on]
  N --> R[CRI runtime: containerd]
  R --> K[kubelet: same cgroup driver]
  K --> C[CNI plugin: pod network]
  K --> V[CSI driver: volumes]

video.title: CRI, CNI, CSI - what's this all about?

notes.objective: Create and manage Kubernetes clusters using kubeadm
notes.title: kubeadm init and join
notes.gist: kubeadm init builds the control plane on one node, you add a CNI plugin, then other nodes run the printed join command.
points: `kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=<cidr>` if your CNI needs it; never overlap host networks.
Copy `/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf` to `$HOME/.kube/config` so kubectl works.
CoreDNS will not start until a CNI pod network add-on is installed.
Workers: `kubeadm join <host>:6443 --token <t> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<h>`.
Lost the join line? `kubeadm token create --print-join-command` prints a fresh one.
notes.tip: Task: join node02 to the cluster. Trap: running join on the control plane, or reusing an expired token instead of printing a new join command.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Prepare nodes] --> B[kubeadm init on control plane]
  B --> C[Copy admin.conf for kubectl]
  C --> D[Install CNI add-on]
  D --> E[kubeadm join on workers]
  E --> F[kubectl get nodes: Ready]

video.title: Setup Kubernetes Cluster Using Kubeadm [Multi-node]

notes.objective: Implement and configure a highly-available control plane
notes.title: Highly available control plane
notes.gist: Run several control plane nodes behind one load-balanced endpoint so losing a node does not stop the API.
points: Stacked: etcd runs on each control plane node; simpler, needs at least three nodes.
External etcd: separate etcd hosts; at least three control plane plus three etcd hosts.
Workers reach `kube-apiserver` through a load balancer in both topologies.
Set `--control-plane-endpoint` at `kubeadm init`; a single-node cluster cannot be converted later.
Stacked risk: losing one node removes an etcd member and an API server together.
notes.tip: Questions ask which topology fits or why a third node matters. Trap: thinking two control plane nodes are HA; etcd stops working without a majority.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  W[Workers and kubectl] --> LB[Load balancer: 6443]
  LB --> C1[Control plane 1 + etcd]
  LB --> C2[Control plane 2 + etcd]
  LB --> C3[Control plane 3 + etcd]

notes.objective: Manage the lifecycle of Kubernetes clusters
notes.title: Upgrade a cluster with kubeadm
notes.gist: Upgrade one minor version at a time: control plane first, then each worker, with kubeadm before kubelet and kubectl.
points: Skipping minor versions is unsupported: 1.36 to 1.37, never 1.35 to 1.37.
With `pkgs.k8s.io`, switch the apt repo to the target minor version first.
`apt-mark unhold kubeadm`, install the exact version, then `apt-mark hold kubeadm` again.
First control plane: `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.x.y`; every other node: `kubeadm upgrade node`.
Drain before a minor kubelet upgrade; `kubeadm upgrade` also renews its certificates.
notes.tip: Full command list is in the playbook. Trap: `upgrade apply` on a worker, kubelet before kubeadm, or skipping `daemon-reload`, restart and uncordon.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Drain node] --> B[Upgrade kubeadm package]
  B --> C{First control plane?}
  C -->|yes| D[kubeadm upgrade apply]
  C -->|no| E[kubeadm upgrade node]
  D --> F[Upgrade kubelet, kubectl, restart]
  E --> F
  F --> G[Uncordon node]

notes.objective: Manage the lifecycle of Kubernetes clusters
notes.title: etcd snapshot backup and restore
notes.gist: etcd holds all cluster state; a snapshot file lets you roll the whole cluster back after data loss or a bad change.
points: Get cert paths from `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml`: `--trusted-ca-file`, `--cert-file`, `--key-file`.
Save with `etcdctl` (talks to etcd); restore and status with `etcdutl` (works on files).
`etcdutl --data-dir <new-dir> snapshot restore snap.db` creates the new directory.
Then point the `etcd-data` hostPath in `etcd.yaml` at that directory.
Check a file: `etcdutl --write-out=table snapshot status snap.db`.
notes.tip: Save and restore commands are in the playbook. Trap: leaving out `--endpoints` or a cert flag so save fails, or restoring into the live data dir.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Read certs from etcd.yaml] --> B[etcdctl snapshot save]
  B --> C[(snapshot.db)]
  C --> D[etcdutl restore: new data dir]
  D --> E[Edit etcd-data hostPath]
  E --> F[kubelet restarts etcd]

notes.objective: Use Helm and Kustomize to install cluster components
notes.title: Helm and Kustomize for components
notes.gist: Helm installs packaged charts as named releases; Kustomize patches plain YAML through a kustomization.yaml, no templates.
points: Helm: `helm repo add <name> <url>`, then `helm install <release> <name>/<chart> -n <ns>`.
`helm list -A` shows releases; `helm uninstall <release>` removes one.
OCI charts need no repo: `helm install <release> oci://<registry>/<chart> --version <v>`.
Kustomize: `kubectl kustomize <dir>` previews; `kubectl apply -k <dir>` applies.
kustomization.yaml lists `resources`, `patches`, `images`, `namePrefix`; generators add a hash suffix.
notes.tip: Tasks name the release, chart version and namespace exactly. Trap: forgetting `-n` or `--version`, or `kubectl apply -f` on a kustomize folder instead of `-k`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Install a component} -->|packaged chart| B[helm repo add, helm install]
  B --> C[Release tracked: helm list]
  A -->|own YAML + overlays| D[kustomization.yaml: resources, patches]
  D --> E[kubectl apply -k dir]

notes.objective: Understand CRDs, install and configure operators
notes.title: CRDs and operators
notes.gist: A CRD adds a new object type to the API; an operator is a controller that watches those objects and acts.
points: A CRD alone only stores data; a custom controller makes it act.
Operator = custom resources plus a controller that encodes operational know-how.
Find them: `kubectl get crd`, then `kubectl explain <kind>.spec` for fields.
Install an operator by applying its CRDs and controller, often with Helm.
CRDs are Namespaced or Cluster scoped and validate with an OpenAPI v3 schema.
notes.tip: Tasks: list an operator's CRDs, or create a custom object from given YAML. Trap: creating the object before its CRD exists, or a wrong `apiVersion` group.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[CRD: new kind] --> B[API server stores objects]
  U([kubectl apply custom object]) --> B
  B --> C[Operator controller watches]
  C --> D[Creates pods, services, config]
  C -.->|updates| E[Object status]

summary.tests: Whether you can build, upgrade, back up and secure a kubeadm cluster, and install add-ons with Helm, Kustomize and CRDs.
must_know: Upgrade one minor version at a time: control plane first, kubeadm before kubelet.
`kubeadm upgrade apply` on the first control plane; `kubeadm upgrade node` everywhere else.
etcd backup needs the endpoint plus three cert flags from the etcd manifest.
Restore into a new data dir, then repoint the `etcd-data` hostPath.
A RoleBinding grants in one namespace, even when it references a ClusterRole.
Verify RBAC with `kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<user>`.
HA needs at least three control plane nodes behind one endpoint.
traps: Using a ClusterRoleBinding when the task limits access to one namespace.
Forgetting to drain, restart kubelet or uncordon during an upgrade.
Applying a kustomize folder with `-f` instead of `-k`.

notes.objective: Understand connectivity between Pods
notes.title: Pod networking model
notes.gist: Every pod gets its own cluster-wide IP and can reach every other pod directly, on any node, without NAT.
points: One IP per pod; containers in the same pod share it and use localhost.
Pod to pod across nodes works without proxies or address translation.
The CNI plugin builds the pod network; kube-proxy implements Service virtual IPs.
Node agents such as the kubelet can reach all pods on their node.
Pod IPs change when pods are replaced, so clients use Services.
notes.tip: Questions ask why pods cannot talk: no CNI installed, or a NetworkPolicy. Trap: blaming the Service when pod-to-pod by IP already fails.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P1[Pod A: own IP] -->|direct, no NAT| P2[Pod B on another node]
  CNI[CNI plugin] -.->|builds pod network| P1
  CNI -.-> P2
  KP[kube-proxy] -.->|Service virtual IPs| S[Service]
  S --> P2

notes.objective: Use ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer service types and endpoints
notes.title: Service types, ports and endpoints
notes.gist: A Service gives a stable name and IP to a changing set of pods chosen by a label selector.
points: ClusterIP is the default and is reachable only inside the cluster.
NodePort opens the same port on every node, default range 30000-32767.
LoadBalancer builds on NodePort and asks the cloud for an external load balancer.
`port` is the Service port; `targetPort` defaults to the same value.
`clusterIP: None` makes a headless Service: DNS returns the pod IPs.
notes.tip: Task: expose a deployment on NodePort 30080. Trap: `kubectl expose` cannot set the nodePort, so edit the Service after; and match `targetPort` to the container port.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C([Client outside]) --> LB[LoadBalancer: cloud LB]
  LB --> NP[NodePort: same port, every node]
  NP --> CIP[ClusterIP: inside only]
  CIP -->|selector| EP[EndpointSlices]
  EP --> P[Pods on targetPort]

video.title: Kubernetes Networking: NodePort, LoadBalancer, Ingress, or Gateway API?

notes.objective: Define and enforce Network Policies
notes.title: NetworkPolicy: isolation and default deny
notes.gist: Pods accept all traffic until a NetworkPolicy selects them; after that only what some policy allows gets through.
points: Needs a CNI that enforces policies; otherwise the object exists but does nothing.
Policies are additive: allowed traffic is the union, and there are no deny rules.
Default deny ingress: `podSelector: {}`, `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, no ingress rules.
A connection needs both the source egress and the destination ingress to allow it.
Egress deny also blocks DNS; allow port 53 UDP and TCP to kube-dns.
notes.tip: Typical: deny all, then allow app to db on one port. Trap: egress rules without DNS break lookups, or the policy lands in the wrong namespace.

video.title: Kubernetes Network Policy Tutorial - yaml explained + Demo Calico

notes.objective: Define and enforce Network Policies
notes.title: NetworkPolicy selectors: AND versus OR
notes.gist: Inside one from item, podSelector and namespaceSelector must both match; written as separate items, either one is enough.
points: One item holding `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` = those pods in those namespaces only.
Two items, each starting with `-`, = either source is allowed.
A bare `podSelector` in `from` only matches pods in the policy's own namespace.
Select a namespace by name with label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name: <ns>`.
See how it was read: `kubectl describe networkpolicy <name>`.
notes.tip: The exam may make you pick the least permissive policy from several files. Trap: one extra dash turns AND into OR and opens a whole namespace.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[from list] --> B{One item with both selectors?}
  B -->|yes| C[AND: matching pods in matching namespaces]
  B -->|no, two items| D[OR: local pods or whole namespaces]

notes.objective: Know how to use Ingress controllers and Ingress resources
notes.title: Ingress: HTTP routing to Services
notes.gist: An Ingress maps hosts and paths to Services, but only a running Ingress controller turns those rules into real routing.
points: Set `ingressClassName` to pick the controller; if omitted, the default IngressClass applies.
Every path needs a `pathType`: `Exact`, `Prefix` or `ImplementationSpecific`.
Prefix `/foo` matches `/foo` and `/foo/bar` but not `/foobar`.
TLS uses a Secret holding cert and key; only port 443 is supported.
The Ingress API is frozen; Gateway API is the recommended successor.
notes.tip: Task: route shop.example.com/api to Service api on 8080. Trap: wrong `ingressClassName`, a port the Service lacks, or the Ingress in another namespace.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C([Client]) --> IC[Ingress controller pod]
  IR[Ingress rules: host, path] -.->|configures| IC
  IC -->|shop.example.com/api| S1[Service api]
  IC -->|no match| S2[Default backend]

video.title: Kubernetes Ingress in 5 mins

notes.objective: Use the Gateway API to manage Ingress traffic
notes.title: Gateway API: classes, gateways, routes
notes.gist: Gateway API splits ingress by role: a class names the controller, a Gateway opens listeners, and Routes send traffic to Services.
points: GatewayClass sets the `controllerName` of the implementation; it usually ships with the controller.
Gateway sets `gatewayClassName` and `listeners` with protocol, port and optional hostname.
HTTPRoute attaches via `parentRefs` to a Gateway and forwards to `backendRefs` Services.
A Gateway accepts Routes from its own namespace only, unless `allowedRoutes` says otherwise.
It is an add-on: its CRDs and a controller must be installed first.
notes.tip: Task: write an HTTPRoute for an existing Gateway, or replace an Ingress. Trap: wrong `parentRefs` name or namespace, or a Route in a namespace the listener rejects.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  GC[GatewayClass: controller] --> GW[Gateway: listeners, port 80]
  R[HTTPRoute: host, path match] -->|parentRefs| GW
  R -->|backendRefs| S[Service]
  S --> P[Pods]

video.title: Kubernetes Gateway API tutorial: 5 examples of what you can do with it

notes.objective: Understand and use CoreDNS
notes.title: DNS names and CoreDNS
notes.gist: CoreDNS gives every Service a predictable name, and each pod searches its own namespace first when resolving short names.
points: Service record `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` gives the ClusterIP; headless returns pod IPs.
Pod `resolv.conf` searches `<ns>.svc.cluster.local` first, so short names work within one namespace.
Pod record: IP with dashes, for example `172-17-0-3.default.pod.cluster.local`.
Config is the Corefile in the `coredns` ConfigMap in `kube-system`; the Service is still `kube-dns`.
Default `dnsPolicy` is ClusterFirst; the value `Default` inherits the node's resolver.
notes.tip: Task: write a Service's FQDN, or add a stub domain with `forward` in the Corefile. Trap: using a short name across namespaces.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P[Pod looks up api.prod] --> R[resolv.conf search list]
  R --> D[kube-dns Service]
  D --> C[CoreDNS pods: Corefile]
  C -->|cluster.local| S[Service ClusterIP]
  C -->|other names| U[Upstream via forward]

video.title: Day 31/40 - Understanding CoreDNS In Kubernetes

summary.tests: Whether you can expose apps with Services, Ingress and Gateway API, restrict traffic with NetworkPolicies, and resolve names through CoreDNS.
must_know: ClusterIP is default; NodePort range 30000-32767; LoadBalancer builds on NodePort.
Empty endpoints mean the selector does not match pod labels.
NetworkPolicies are additive allow lists and need a CNI that enforces them.
One `from` item with both selectors is AND; two items are OR.
Ingress needs a controller, an `ingressClassName` and a `pathType` on every path.
Gateway API: GatewayClass, Gateway with listeners, HTTPRoute with `parentRefs` and `backendRefs`.
FQDN `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`; short names resolve only in the same namespace.
traps: An egress deny policy that forgets DNS on port 53.
A stray dash in a NetworkPolicy `from` list that widens access.
Ingress, Route or policy created in a different namespace from its target.

video.title: How Kubernetes deployments work

domains.diagram:
flowchart LR
  DEP[Deployment] --> RS[ReplicaSet]
  RS --> P1[Pod]
  RS --> P2[Pod]
  DEP -->|rolling update, rollback| RS2[New ReplicaSet]
  P1 --> SCH{Scheduler}
  SCH -->|requests, nodeSelector, affinity, taints + tolerations| N[(Node)]
  CMS[ConfigMap / Secret] -.-> P1
  HPA[HPA] -.-> DEP

notes.objective: Understand application deployments and how to perform rolling update and rollbacks
notes.title: Rolling updates and rollbacks
notes.gist: Changing a Deployment's pod template starts a rollout to a new ReplicaSet; a rollback switches back to an older one.
points: Only `.spec.template` changes create a revision; scaling does not.
Defaults: `maxUnavailable` 25% and `maxSurge` 25%; `Recreate` kills all pods first.
`kubectl rollout history deploy/<d>` lists revisions; add `--revision=N` for details.
`kubectl rollout undo deploy/<d> --to-revision=N` returns to a chosen revision.
`revisionHistoryLimit` keeps 10 old ReplicaSets; set CHANGE-CAUSE with the `kubernetes.io/change-cause` annotation.
notes.tip: Task: update the image, then roll back to revision 2. Trap: wrong container name in `kubectl set image`, or undoing without checking `rollout history` first.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D[Deployment] --> RS1[ReplicaSet rev 1: old pods]
  D -->|template change| RS2[ReplicaSet rev 2: new pods]
  RS1 -.->|scaled down step by step| X[Old pods gone]
  RS2 -.->|scaled up step by step| Y[New pods ready]
  D -->|rollout undo| RS1

notes.objective: Understand the primitives used to create robust, self-healing, application deployments
notes.title: Self-healing: controllers, restarts, probes
notes.gist: Controllers keep the desired pod count, the kubelet restarts failed containers, and probes decide restarts and traffic.
points: A ReplicaSet, managed by a Deployment, replaces deleted or lost pods to match `replicas`.
`restartPolicy`: Always (default), OnFailure or Never; Jobs use OnFailure or Never.
Liveness fails: container restarted. Readiness fails: pod IP removed from Service endpoints.
A startup probe holds off liveness and readiness until the app has started.
A bare pod is not recreated if its node dies; use a controller.
notes.tip: Task: add a liveness probe on /healthz port 8080. Trap: adding readiness when a restart was asked for, or a probe port that differs from the container.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Container unhealthy] --> B{Which probe failed?}
  B -->|liveness| C[kubelet restarts container]
  B -->|startup| C
  B -->|readiness| D[Removed from endpoints]
  E[Pod or node lost] --> F[ReplicaSet creates replacement]

video.title: Kubernetes Health Checks: Liveness vs. Readiness vs. Startup Probe

notes.objective: Use ConfigMaps and Secrets to configure applications
notes.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets into pods
notes.gist: Keep settings outside the image in a ConfigMap or Secret, then feed them to pods as environment variables or mounted files.
points: `kubectl create configmap app --from-literal=MODE=prod --from-file=app.conf`.
`kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=pass=x`; values are base64, not encrypted.
One key: `env[].valueFrom.configMapKeyRef`; every key: `envFrom` with `configMapRef`.
Mounted volumes update automatically; env vars and `subPath` mounts need a pod restart.
ConfigMap data is limited to 1 MiB; `immutable: true` blocks changes.
notes.tip: Task: mount a ConfigMap as files in /etc/app, or expose one Secret key as an env var. Trap: key name typos, or expecting env vars to refresh.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  CM[ConfigMap] -->|env, envFrom| E[Env vars: fixed at start]
  SE[Secret] -->|secretKeyRef| E
  CM -->|volume| F[Files: auto-update]
  SE -->|volume| F
  E --> C[Container]
  F --> C

video.title: Kubernetes ConfigMap and Secret as Kubernetes Volumes | Demo

notes.objective: Configure workload autoscaling
notes.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
notes.gist: The HPA adds or removes replicas so average usage stays near a target, using metrics served by metrics-server.
points: `kubectl autoscale deploy web --min=2 --max=8 --cpu=70%`; older kubectl uses `--cpu-percent=70`.
Needs metrics-server and CPU requests on the pods, or utilization is undefined.
desired = ceil(current replicas x current metric / target); skipped within 10% tolerance.
Checks every 15 seconds; scale-down uses a 5 minute stabilization window by default.
`autoscaling/v2` adds memory, custom metrics and a `behavior` section.
notes.tip: Task: HPA at 50% CPU, 2 to 5 replicas. Trap: target shows unknown because pods have no CPU requests or metrics-server is not running.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  MS[metrics-server] --> H[HPA: checks every 15s]
  H --> Q{Usage vs target}
  Q -->|above| U[Scale up]
  Q -->|below, after 5 min| D2[Scale down]
  U --> DEP[Deployment replicas]
  D2 --> DEP

notes.objective: Configure Pod admission and scheduling (limits, node affinity, etc.)
notes.title: Requests, limits, LimitRange, ResourceQuota
notes.gist: Requests reserve capacity for scheduling, limits cap use at runtime, and LimitRange and ResourceQuota enforce rules per namespace.
points: The scheduler places a pod only where free allocatable covers its requests; else Pending.
Over the CPU limit: throttled. Over the memory limit: OOM killed.
CPU in cores or millicores like `500m`; memory in bytes with `Mi` or `Gi`.
LimitRange sets per-container defaults and min or max; ResourceQuota caps namespace totals.
`kubectl set resources deploy/web --requests=cpu=100m --limits=memory=256Mi`.
notes.tip: Task: give a pod 100m CPU request and 128Mi limit. Trap: a ResourceQuota on CPU or memory rejects pods that omit requests or limits; read the quota first.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  P[Pod requests and limits] --> L1[LimitRange: defaults, min, max]
  L1 --> Q[ResourceQuota: namespace totals]
  Q --> S{Node has free allocatable?}
  S -->|yes| R[Scheduled, limits enforced]
  S -->|no| PE[Pending]

video.title: Day 16/40 - Kubernetes Requests and Limits - CKA Full Course 2025

source.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

notes.objective: Configure Pod admission and scheduling (limits, node affinity, etc.)
notes.title: nodeSelector and node affinity
notes.gist: Label nodes, then make pods require or prefer those labels; this pulls pods toward nodes, while taints push them away.
points: `kubectl label node n1 disktype=ssd`, then `nodeSelector: {disktype: ssd}` in the pod spec.
`requiredDuringScheduling...` is a hard rule; `preferred...` uses weights from 1 to 100.
Several `nodeSelectorTerms` are ORed; expressions inside one term are ANDed.
IgnoredDuringExecution: later label changes do not evict running pods.
`nodeName` bypasses the scheduler completely, taints included.
notes.tip: Task: run only on nodes labelled zone=east. Trap: placing affinity outside `spec.template.spec` in a Deployment, or a label key typo leaving pods Pending.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  N[Label node: disktype=ssd] --> S{Pod rule type}
  S -->|required| H[Only matching nodes, else Pending]
  S -->|preferred, weight| P[Matching nodes score higher]
  S -->|nodeName| B[Scheduler bypassed]

video.title: Kubernetes Affinity and Anti Affinity vs NodeSelector (Examples)

notes.objective: Configure Pod admission and scheduling (limits, node affinity, etc.)
notes.title: Taints and tolerations
notes.gist: A taint keeps pods off a node unless they carry a matching toleration; a toleration permits, it does not attract.
points: `kubectl taint node n1 gpu=true:NoSchedule`; add a trailing `-` to remove it.
NoSchedule blocks new pods; PreferNoSchedule is soft; NoExecute also evicts running pods.
With NoExecute, `tolerationSeconds` keeps a pod that long before eviction.
Toleration `operator` defaults to Equal; `Exists` matches any value and takes no value.
kubeadm control plane nodes carry `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule`.
notes.tip: Task: run a pod on the tainted node. Trap: a toleration alone may still land elsewhere; add nodeSelector or affinity, and match key, value and effect exactly.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  T[Node taint gpu=true:NoSchedule] --> Q{Pod tolerates it?}
  Q -->|no| X[Never scheduled there]
  Q -->|yes| Y[Allowed there, not forced]
  Y --> A[Add affinity to pin it]

video.title: Kubernetes For Beginners: Taints & Tolerations

summary.tests: Whether you can roll out and roll back Deployments, configure apps with ConfigMaps and Secrets, autoscale, and control where pods land.
must_know: Only pod template changes create a revision; `rollout undo --to-revision` rolls back.
Rolling update defaults: 25% max unavailable, 25% max surge.
ConfigMap env vars do not refresh; mounted files do, except `subPath` mounts.
HPA needs metrics-server and CPU requests; scale-down waits 5 minutes by default.
Requests drive scheduling; CPU over limit is throttled, memory over limit is OOM killed.
Affinity attracts pods, taints repel them, tolerations only permit.
NoExecute evicts running pods; NoSchedule only blocks new ones.
traps: Putting nodeSelector, tolerations or probes outside `spec.template.spec` in a Deployment.
Expecting a toleration alone to place a pod on one specific node.
HPA target stuck at unknown because the pods have no CPU requests.

video.title: How volumes and storage work in Kubernetes

domains.diagram:
flowchart LR
  POD[Pod volumeMounts] --> PVC[PersistentVolumeClaim: size, accessMode]
  PVC -->|bind| PV[PersistentVolume]
  SC[StorageClass: provisioner, reclaimPolicy] -->|dynamic provisioning| PV
  PV --> DISK[(Disk, NFS, CSI)]

notes.objective: Manage persistent volumes and persistent volume claims
notes.title: PV and PVC binding
notes.gist: A PV is a piece of storage, a PVC is a request for it, and Kubernetes binds matching pairs one to one.
points: Binding needs enough size, a matching access mode and the same `storageClassName`.
No match: the PVC stays Pending until a suitable PV appears.
Static PV without a class: set `storageClassName: ""` on the PVC, or the default class applies.
Pod side: `volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName` plus a matching `volumeMounts` entry.
A PVC in use by a pod is only removed after the pod is gone.
notes.tip: Task: create a PV, a PVC and a pod mounting it at /data. Trap: PVC Pending from a class or access mode mismatch; `kubectl describe pvc` says which.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P[Pod: volumeMounts at /data] --> C[PVC: size, mode, class]
  C --> Q{Matching PV?}
  Q -->|no| PE[PVC stays Pending]
  Q -->|yes, 1:1| V[PV: capacity, mode, class]
  V --> D[(Disk, NFS, hostPath)]

video.title: Kubernetes Volumes 2:  Understanding Persistent Volume (PV) and Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)

notes.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
notes.title: Access modes: RWO, ROX, RWX, RWOP
notes.gist: Access modes say how many nodes or pods may mount a volume and whether they may write to it.
points: RWO ReadWriteOnce: read-write by one node; pods on that node can share it.
ROX ReadOnlyMany: read-only on many nodes. RWX ReadWriteMany: read-write on many nodes.
RWOP ReadWriteOncePod: exactly one pod in the whole cluster.
Modes drive PV and PVC matching; a volume mounts with one mode at a time.
Backend decides support: hostPath is RWO only, NFS supports RWX.
notes.tip: Questions ask which mode lets replicas on different nodes write. Trap: choosing RWO, which ties the volume to one node, or thinking modes enforce write protection.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  Q{Who needs to mount it?} -->|one pod only| A[RWOP]
  Q -->|pods on one node| B[RWO]
  Q -->|many nodes, read only| C[ROX]
  Q -->|many nodes, read write| D[RWX]

notes.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
notes.title: Reclaim policies and PV phases
notes.gist: The reclaim policy decides what happens to a PV and its data once its claim is deleted.
points: Retain: the PV becomes Released and keeps its data; an admin cleans up by hand.
Delete: removes the PV object and the backing storage asset.
Recycle is deprecated; use dynamic provisioning instead.
Dynamic PVs take the StorageClass `reclaimPolicy`, which defaults to Delete.
Phases: Available, Bound, Released, Failed. Change policy with `kubectl patch pv` on `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy`.
notes.tip: Task: make sure data survives PVC deletion. Trap: a Released PV will not bind a new claim until its old `claimRef` is cleared.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Available] -->|PVC binds| B[Bound]
  B -->|PVC deleted| C{reclaimPolicy}
  C -->|Retain| R[Released: data kept]
  C -->|Delete| X[PV and disk removed]
  R -.->|admin clears claimRef| A

notes.objective: Implement storage classes and dynamic volume provisioning
notes.title: StorageClass and dynamic provisioning
notes.gist: A StorageClass tells a provisioner how to create PVs on demand, so a PVC naming the class gets a fresh volume.
points: Fields: `provisioner` (required), `parameters`, `reclaimPolicy` (default Delete), `allowVolumeExpansion`.
Default class: annotation `storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"`; class-less PVCs use it.
`volumeBindingMode` defaults to Immediate; `WaitForFirstConsumer` waits for a pod and its node.
With WaitForFirstConsumer, a pod using `nodeName` leaves the PVC Pending.
Growing a PVC works only if its class has `allowVolumeExpansion: true`.
notes.tip: Task: create a class and make it the default. Trap: two default classes, or treating a WaitForFirstConsumer PVC as broken while it waits for a pod.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  PVC[PVC: storageClassName fast] --> SC[StorageClass fast]
  SC --> PR[Provisioner, CSI driver]
  PR --> PV[New PV, bound]
  SC -.->|WaitForFirstConsumer| W[Waits for a pod first]

notes.objective: Configure volume types, access modes and reclaim policies
notes.title: Volume types: emptyDir, hostPath, local
notes.gist: Pick a volume by lifetime: emptyDir lives with the pod, hostPath and local tie data to a node, PVCs outlive pods.
points: emptyDir: created empty when scheduled, survives container crashes, deleted when the pod leaves.
`emptyDir.medium: Memory` uses RAM; set `sizeLimit` to cap it.
hostPath mounts a node path and is risky; `type: DirectoryOrCreate` creates it if missing.
`local` volumes are static PVs only, with node affinity; no dynamic provisioning.
Share files between containers by mounting one emptyDir in both.
notes.tip: Task: app and sidecar share logs through an emptyDir. Trap: names differ between `volumes` and `volumeMounts`, or expecting emptyDir data after pod deletion.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  Q{How long must data live?} -->|pod lifetime| E[emptyDir]
  Q -->|tied to one node| H[hostPath or local PV]
  Q -->|beyond the pod| P[PVC bound to PV]
  E --> S[Shared by containers in pod]

summary.tests: Whether you can create PVs, PVCs and StorageClasses, mount them in pods, and choose the right access mode and reclaim policy.
must_know: A PVC binds a PV only when size, access mode and class all match.
An unmatched PVC stays Pending; `kubectl describe pvc` shows why.
RWO is one node, RWOP is one pod, RWX is many nodes writing.
Retain keeps data and leaves the PV Released; Delete removes PV and disk.
StorageClass `reclaimPolicy` defaults to Delete; binding mode defaults to Immediate.
WaitForFirstConsumer delays binding until a pod uses the PVC.
emptyDir data is gone once the pod leaves its node.
traps: A static PV with no class, while the PVC silently gets the default StorageClass.
Treating a WaitForFirstConsumer PVC in Pending as broken.
Expecting a Released PV to bind again without clearing its `claimRef`.

commands.what: If ENDPOINTS is empty, the selector does not match the pod labels.

A throwaway pod that curls the service by DNS name. --rm deletes it when it exits.

Deployment in one line. Add --dry-run=client -o yaml to get a manifest.
Service from a Deployment. --port is the service port, --target-port the container port.

A Role is namespaced; ClusterRole is cluster-wide.
Bind the role to a ServiceAccount (or --user=jane).
Verify as that identity. Answers yes or no.
The three cert flags come from the etcd static pod manifest (kubectl describe pod etcd-<node> -n kube-system).
Restore into a new directory, then point the etcd manifest's hostPath at it.

commands.cmd: kubectl drain <cp> --ignore-daemonsets; sudo apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.3x.y-*; sudo kubeadm upgrade plan; sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.3x.y

commands.what: Then kubelet and kubectl, restart, uncordon. Workers: kubeadm upgrade node instead of apply.
Status Bound means the PVC found a PV. Pending means no PV matches size, access mode or storageClassName.
Events say why it is not binding.
Ingress in one line; add --annotation for rewrites.
Gateway API objects (new curriculum).
DNS check from inside a pod.

commands.cmd: alias k=kubectl; export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'; export now='--force --grace-period=0'
commands.what: Type k run x --image=nginx $do > x.yaml. The aliases save minutes.

commands.cmd: grep -n <text> file; sed -i 's/old/new/' file; tail -f /var/log/x; cat file | less

commands.cmd: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[].metadata.name'; kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName
commands.what: Pull specific fields when a task asks you to write names to a file.
